summary: This note traces the language status of Madagascar, covering the Malagasy language's dialects and the shifting official-language rules from the 1958 Constitution through the 2010 referendum. It explains how French gained official status under colonial rule, how the 1992 and 2007 constitutions treated Malagasy, French and English, and how a 2000 court case and the 2010 referendum shaped policy. The note also records that the political opposition does not recognize the 2010 referendum outcome.
one_line: Overview of Malagasy and French language status and official-language changes in Madagascar's constitutions from 1958 to 2010.
key_facts: The Malagasy language is of Malayo-Polynesian origin and is generally spoken throughout Madagascar.
Numerous Malagasy dialects are generally mutually intelligible and can be clustered into eastern Malagasy and western Malagasy subgroups.
Eastern Malagasy is spoken along the eastern forests and highlands, including the Merina dialect of Antananarivo.
Western Malagasy is spoken across the western coastal plains.
French became the official language during the colonial period, when Madagascar came under the authority of France.
The first national Constitution of 1958 named Malagasy and French as the official languages of the Malagasy Republic.
Madagascar is a francophone country where French is mostly spoken as a second language among the educated population and used for international communication.
The Constitution of 1992 recorded no official languages, although Malagasy was identified as the national language.
In April 2000, a citizen initiated a legal case against the state on the grounds that publishing official documents only in French was unconstitutional.
The High Constitutional Court observed that, in the absence of a language law, French still had the character of an official language.
The Constitution of 2007 kept Malagasy as the national language and reintroduced Malagasy, French, and English as official languages.
English was removed as an official language from the constitution approved by voters in the November 2010 referendum.
The political opposition does not recognize the outcome of the 2010 referendum.
The opposition cites lack of transparency and inclusiveness in how the election was organized by the High Transitional Authority.
